articles.text: The Piedmont Post has named former mayor Bob McBain as its Man of the Year. After serving nearly nine years on the city council, the most recent three years as mayor. In his last official City Council meeting on December 7, McBain modestly pointed to city staff and councilmembers as the reason for successes under his tenure as mayor. McBain said that he was confident in the financial state of the city as outgoing mayor, the result of vigorous work for the duration of his 8-1/2 years on council. Many notable residents and former city staff poured in during public comment to offer their thanks to McBain, including former mayor Dean Barbieri, former City Administrator Paul Benoit, and former piedmont Beautification Foundation President Patty Siskind, among others. articles.text: Piedmont Post is naming University of California, San Francisco Epidemiologist, and Piedmont resident, George Rutherford as its Citizen of the Year. Dr. Rutherford became somewhat of a hero in town in much the same way that Dr. Anthony Fauci became a hero nationwide. Rutherford kept residents abreast of any and all medical advancements and responses to COVID-19 through multiple public forums. Some forums were more condensed and specific. Rutherford was called on by the League of Women Voters to offer his knowledge of the emerging pandemic early in its far-reaching impact. He also spoke during a UCSFhosted medical panel on the possibility of reopening schools. He has appeared several times at the school board meeting to offer advice on safe practices for reopening classes. Rutherford made himself available for Post interviews, even as many Bay Area stations contacted him for insights throughout the pandemic. He continues to be a leading expert and source for many Bay Area, and nationwide, news services. Piedmont resident, epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford.

articles.text: Editor: I am a parent to two PUSD students, as well as a spouse to a PUSD teacher. The COVID-19 pandemic has been incredibly difficult for our entire community, and the frustration everyone is feeling is natural and understandable. The recent anonymous letter to the editor advocating for donations to be withheld from the Piedmont Education Foundation, however, misplaces that frustration and is ultimately irresponsible and self-defeating. It’s important to point out that funds raised by the PEF allows PUSD to create the superior academic, emotional, creative, and social programs that help make PUSD such an awesome district, and these programs would likely not be as robust otherwise. When you factor in the inevitable budget cuts that are no doubt looming in the next couple of years from the economic impact of the pandemic, depriving the district of these additional funds will hurt only one constituency; our children. I have not always supported the decisions that have been made during this time, and I have thought that some stances taken by the district, by the teachers’ union, and by the parent community have been problematic and inconsistent. I will continue to give to PEF because when all of this is over, I want every tool available to those who have always taken great care in providing an exceptional educational environment. Regardless of my opposition to stances taken by the various communities connected to the district, I do believe that they have been operating with the intention of doing what is best for the children. Had the district opened early on, it is likely that we would have experienced the same chaos of intermittent openings and closings as has been the case with many other districts who have opened too soon or without proper planning. There is evidence now that children can safely go back to school, which is good news, and many of us support. Doing that, however, is complicated and not entirely up to the district, the teachers’ union, nor the parent community. We have to follow state and county mandates, as well as the best practices laid out by the various authorities who are doing their best to develop guidelines for constantly shifting circumstances. People should always give as their consciences and financial circumstances dictate, but I for one will be continuing to invest in our children through the institutions that have consistently supported them. –Spencer Perry
articles.title: Criticism of school donations seen as misplaced

Racial injustice. Political turmoil. Economic uncertainty. The list is long. Thus, it was something of a relief, something of a small victory, to prepare the December 2020 preaching and worship schedule for our church newsletter. The birth of every child needs to be greeted as a sign of God’s will that the world go on, as a sign of God’s promise to save and to bless. articles.text: I strongly disagree. In fact, it seems odd to me that the city would not extend the lease. The Center for the Arts has been a success, offering a rare space for visual artists, musicians and actors to show their work and perform. It also provides a wonderful – an exceptional – activity for people in the community and the East Bay, and right in our city. For example, we were treated to “The Sky’s the Limit,” an exhibition of dozens of artist Michael Stehr’s oil paintings, carefully organized so that it was Covid safe. It was great! As a realtor, I always mention the Center to buyers as one of the perks of living in Piedmont. As I understand it, the Center is run by a board of directors who are volunteers. I think they are doing an excellent job. They search and encourage local talent and use their connections to bring talent from faraway, balancing and curating usage by Piedmont talent – including the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the Piedmont Art fundraisers for the schools, youth rehearsals, youth recitals – and also some of the finest talent in the Bay Area and nationally. They have even hosted several international musicians. And before Covid-19 closed many public events, the calendar was full throughout the year. They also seem to do a great job of maintaining and operating the venue. The building has never looked better! And I understand their books are balanced and they are in good financial shape. With an operation that is so well run and serving a very useful public good, why wouldn’t the city extend their lease? In this time of Covid-19, we need the inspiration of artistic groups which are struggling to stay alive. I think now, more than ever, we need to support them. They provide beauty, humor and insights when times are tough. So, extend the PCA’s lease. It would be very sad – and I think a big mistake – to lose this exceptional part of our city. –Carol Brown

articles.text: The following letter was sent to the City Council. Editor: I am writing to express my strong support for allowing the Piedmont Center for the Arts to continue to lease the space at 801 Magnolia Avenue. The Piedmont Center for the Arts provides invaluable local access to the arts for many young people and families in the area. My teenaged daughter, who has played violin since kindergarten, has participated in several studio performances and a master class at the Center, along with the other members of her Quartet. Having an inviting and centrally located venue that supports arts appreciation and performance is especially needed now for young people, for whom the arts provide a place of creativity, connection, and accomplishment during complex and challenging times. With the closure of the Montclair Women’s Art Center in 2015, the role of the Piedmont Center for the Arts in providing a community gathering place for the arts is especially important. It would be a great loss for families in the area if this community treasure were not to continue. Thank you for your consideration. Sincerely, –Jane Wellenkamp, Ph.D.
articles.title: Center for the Arts a nurturing venue for young artists

articles.text: What we won’t miss – from ‘Doomscrolling’ to ‘Blursday’ Commentary by Chris Honoré I recently read an article by New York Times reporter Tim Herrera which made the point that language is dynamic, perpetually responsive to our ever-trending pop culture and contemporary experiences. As a result, we have a vocabulary born of our health care and political crises. Find below a list of these words with definitions. Some I have used as springboards, others I’ve embellished with levity where appropriate, while a few are my own, gleaned from my sofa-bound travels. Let’s begin with Doomscrolling: unedited, online consuming of bad news and information known to be detrimental to one’s mental health and wellbeing. Quarantini: your go-to drink for lockdowns and beyond. The Messy Threshhold: how tidy, clean, put-away, vacuumed, dusted, organized does your now all too familiar digs have to be before it reaches a critical mass of good grief! intolerance. Ditto your Stay at Home Oufit: T-shirt scuzzy? Stand up, take off, turn inside out, put back on (try to get the label in back). You are now Zoom ready. And speaking of Zoom, the online, go-to remote, full-screen interaction and conferencing. No worries – frayed jeans/blown out sweat pants and flip-flops are de rigueur. Maskine: irritation and pimples developed from wearing a mask. Masks, those 4” x 11” piece of protective material, determined to be two-way safety gear, has gone totemic, its defiant absence has devolved into a political statement. As well, while wearing a mask, we’re all trying to say with our eyes and eyebrows what we once said with our grin, smile, and a flash of teeth. Behind the mask, shaving and flossing and fuzz removal are so yesterday. Remote learning, as if. Faceto-face teaching, finally acknowledged as an art, one requiring a trifecta of skill sets that not everyone possesses, long underrated and underpaid, and now suddenly viewed through a different prism. Just ask parents after two weeks of school closures and their attempts at being stand-ins for teachers. Pods: your designated group deemed safe to hang out with. Voter Fraud: non-existent, except in Trump world where unicorns have free range. Blursday: the unreliability of pandemic time, days steeped in déjà vu and all things groundhog-esque, often measured by the aging, brown-pocked bananas in a bowl in the kitchen. And then there’s Social Contact Tracing: trying to remember who you actually had a conversation with… was that this morning or yesterday? Flatten the Curve: not likely. For reasons that are inexplicable, millions of Americans traveled over Thanksgiving and Christmas (aka Superspreaders), refused to social distance or wear masks, which, in the aggregate, are, apparently, a bridge too far. Flattening the Curve proved to be eminently elusive hence, the graphs go vertical as Spikes or Surges. The term Superspreader was often used to characterize Trump’s ubiquitous rallies. It is now used to define holidays such as Thanksgiving and Christmas, when 85 million Americans were reported to have travelled over Christmas. Not exactly a lockdown. Edibles: Arizona, Montana, New Jersey, and South Dakota just legalized marijuana. Timing is everything. While some may reach for a comfort doobie, in the first six months of the pandemic some 19 million Americans bought guns. Feeling more relaxed? Streamers: Can you hear me now? A cohort of not camera shy denizens who sit for hours before a screen and over-share a spectrum of content, from baking to sleeping (really), apparently filling a niche. One streaming site is called “Twitch,” a perfect name for that tic likely to develop after dedicated watching. Editor: I am writing to express my strong support for allowing the Piedmont Center for the Arts to continue to lease the space at 801 Magnolia Avenue. The Piedmont Center for the Arts provides invaluable local access to the arts for many young people and families in the area. My teenaged daughter, who has played violin since kindergarten, has participated in several studio performances and a master class at the Center, along with the other members of her Quartet. Having an inviting and centrally located venue that supports arts appreciation and performance is especially needed now for young people, for whom the arts provide a place of creativity, connection, and accomplishment during complex and challenging times. With the closure of the Montclair Women’s Art Center in 2015, the role of the Piedmont Center for the Arts in providing a community gathering place for the arts is especially important. It would be a great loss for families in the area if this community treasure were not to continue. Thank you for your consideration. Sincerely, –Jane Wellenkamp, Ph.D. Extend the lease for Center for the Arts Editor: I think the city should extend the lease for the Piedmont Center for the Arts. I read an unsolicited email, as well as an opinion piece on the Piedmont Civic Association website, in which someone opposes extending the lease. LETTERS MAIN I strongly disagree. In fact, it seems odd to me that the city would not extend the lease. The Center for the Arts has been a success, offering a rare space for visual artists, musicians and actors to show their work and perform. It also provides a wonderful – an exceptional – activity for people in the community and the East Bay, and right in our city. For example, we were treated to “The Sky’s the Limit,” an exhibition of dozens of artist Michael Stehr’s oil paintings, carefully organized so that it was Covid safe. It was great! As a realtor, I always mention the Center to buyers as one of the perks of living in Piedmont. As I understand it, the Center is run by a board of directors who are volunteers. I think they are doing an excellent job. They search and encourage local talent and use their connections to bring talent from faraway, balancing and curating usage by Piedmont talent – including the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the Piedmont Art fundraisers for the schools, youth rehearsals, youth recitals – and also some of the finest talent in the Bay Area and nationally. They have even hosted several international musicians. And before Covid-19 closed many public events, the calendar was full throughout the year. They also seem to do a great job of maintaining and operating the venue. The building has never looked better! And I understand their books are balanced and they are in good financial shape. With an operation that is so well run and serving a very useful public good, why wouldn’t the city extend their lease? articles.text: History will remember 2020 as a year of devastating wildfires that burned around California and the western United States. An estimated 4 percent of California burned during the worst wildfire season in modern history. Even though Piedmont was spared from the fires, the City suffered through weeks of poor air quality and unearthly hazy conditions due to fire debris in the air hundreds of miles from the actual fires. The San Francisco Bay Area wildfire season took over national headlines in mid-August, when lightning sparked a trio of wildfires that ended up burning for weeks. Within days, two of the fires grew to historically large sizes. The CZU Lightning Complex burned between San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties. The LNU Lightning Complex, the deadliest and most destructive of the three fires, burned in Napa and Sonoma counties. The SCU Lightning Complex burned in rural Stanislaus and San Joaquin counties. In Piedmont, smoke from these fires severely impacted air quality. On August 19, 2020, the recorded air quality in the Bay Area was the worst in the world. The National Weather Service declared a Red Flag Warning, meaning high wildfire risk, for two days in Piedmont in late August, and again on September 7-9. The Bay Area Air Quality Management District declared a record-breaking 30 consecutive days of “Spare the Air” alerts from August 18 to September 17. These alerts mean that particulate pollution in the Bay Area is elevated, making air quality unhealthy. When an alert is declared, the use of fireplaces, wood stoves and outdoor fire pits is prohibited. The number of consecutive Spare the Air days in 2020 was over double the previous record of 14 days of Spare the Air alerts set in 2018. Another 24-hour Spare the Air Alert was declared on October 6, while another alert was issued October 10-12. more than 3.2 million acres had burned in California, and historic high for the U.S. Blazes also ravaged Oregon and Washington. Smoke from these fires caused terrible air quality in the Bay Area. The severe situation was strikingly evident on Wednesday, September 9, when Piedmont skies turned a dark orange color. Although the color dissipated, the unhealthy air conditions continued for days. Also in September, Piedmont firefighters joined others in battling the Creek Fire burning through the Sierra Nevada mountains near Fresno. On October 13, a Red Flag Warning was issued for the East Bay Hills through October 16. On October 14, PG&E began notifying some Alameda County residents, including the Montclair neighborhood of Oakland, in October about a potential Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) due to wildfire risk. More Red Flag Warnings were issued for the East Bay Hills from October 21 to October 23. The entire Bay Area, including Piedmont, was put under a Red Flag Warning on October 25 as hurricane force gusts blew through the region. That day, the NWS measured gusts over 50 miles per hour in Piedmont, where winds knocked down tree branches. In Mount Diablo to the east of Piedmont, 70 miles per hour gusts were recorded. The August Complex Fire, sparked by lightning in August, burned in and around the Mendocino National Forest. It was the largest wildfire in California history and became the state’s first “gigafire” in late October. A gigafire means a wildfire that burns over 1 million acres. In October, a fire in Montclair ignited two homes and some vegetation. No one was hurt but several people were displaced. Some homes on the eastern edge of Piedmont were impacted by a scheduled PSPS on October 25. Several dozen customers in the City reported a loss of power for several days. Cooler, wetter weather moved into the region in November, but wildfire risks continued. The August Complex Fire was declared 100 percent contained by Cal Fire on November 12 after burning a total of 1,032,648 acres. Risks continued even into December of 2020. A rare Red Flag Warning was issued for the East Bay Hills by NWS from December 6 to December 7. There have been only two other December Red Flag Warnings in Bay Area history, both within the past decade – 2013 and 2017. At the height of drought conditions in California – in the 2010s – Red Flag Warnings were occasionally ordered in January. Meteorologists believe it is possible the region could see some Red Flag Warnings issued next month. As of yesterday, December 29, six of 12 Cal Fire units in Northern California had begun winter preparations, traditionally a signal that the wildfire season is over.
articles.title: 2020 – worst wildfire year in California history

An estimated 4 percent of California burned during the worst wildfire season in modern history. Even though Piedmont was spared from the fires, the City suffered through weeks of poor air quality and unearthly hazy conditions due to fire debris in the air hundreds of miles from the actual fires. The San Francisco Bay Area wildfire season took over national headlines in mid-August, when lightning sparked a trio of wildfires that ended up burning for weeks. Within days, two of the fires grew to historically large sizes. The CZU Lightning Complex burned between San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties. The LNU Lightning Complex, the deadliest and most destructive of the three fires, burned in Napa and Sonoma counties. The SCU Lightning Complex burned in rural Stanislaus and San Joaquin counties. In Piedmont, smoke from these fires severely impacted air quality. On August 19, 2020, the recorded air quality in the Bay Area was the worst in the world. The National Weather Service declared a Red Flag Warning, meaning high wildfire risk, for two days in Piedmont in late August, and again on September 7-9. The Bay Area Air Quality Management District declared a record-breaking 30 consecutive days of “Spare the Air” alerts from August 18 to September 17. These alerts mean that particulate pollution in the Bay Area is elevated, making air quality unhealthy. When an alert is declared, the use of fireplaces, wood stoves and outdoor fire pits is prohibited. The number of consecutive Spare the Air days in 2020 was over double the previous record of 14 days of Spare the Air alerts set in 2018. Another 24-hour Spare the Air Alert was declared on October 6, while another alert was issued October 10-12. By the middle of September, more than 3.2 million acres had burned in California, and historic high for the U.S. Blazes also ravaged Oregon and Washington. Smoke from these fires caused terrible air quality in the Bay Area. The severe situation was strikingly evident on Wednesday, September 9, when Piedmont skies turned a dark orange color. Although the color dissipated, the unhealthy air conditions continued for days. Also in September, Piedmont firefighters joined others in battling the Creek Fire burning through the Sierra Nevada mountains near Fresno. On October 13, a Red Flag Warning was issued for the East Bay Hills through October 16. On October 14, PG&E began notifying some Alameda County residents, including the Montclair neighborhood of Oakland, in October about a potential Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) due to wildfire risk. More Red Flag Warnings were issued for the East Bay Hills from October 21 to October 23. The entire Bay Area, including Piedmont, was put under a Red Flag Warning on October 25 as hurricane force gusts blew through the region. That day, the NWS measured gusts over 50 miles per hour in Piedmont, where winds knocked down tree branches. In Mount Diablo to the east of Piedmont, 70 miles per hour gusts were recorded. The August Complex Fire, sparked by lightning in August, burned in and around the Mendocino National Forest. It was the largest wildfire in California history and became the state’s first “gigafire” in late October. A gigafire means a wildfire that burns over 1 million acres. In October, a fire in Montclair ignited two homes and some vegetation. No one was hurt but several people were displaced. Some homes on the eastern edge of Piedmont were impacted by a scheduled PSPS on October 25. Several dozen customers in the City reported a loss of power for several days. Cooler, wetter weather moved into the region in November, but wildfire risks continued. The August Complex Fire was declared 100 percent contained by Cal Fire on November 12 after burning a total of 1,032,648 acres. Risks continued even into December of 2020. A rare Red Flag Warning was issued for the East Bay Hills by NWS from December 6 to December 7. There have been only two other December Red Flag Warnings in Bay Area history, both within the past decade – 2013 and 2017. At the height of drought conditions in California – in the 2010s – Red Flag Warnings were occasionally ordered in January. Meteorologists believe it is possible the region could see some Red Flag Warnings issued next month. As of yesterday, December 29, six of 12 Cal Fire units in Northern California had begun winter preparations, traditionally a signal that the wildfire season is over. articles.text: Jazz band saxophonist. Rock band member. Composer. YouTube musician. Self-taught guitarist, drummer and pianist. As if that weren’t impressive enough for a 17-year-old, Piedmont High School senior Connor Stratman has yet another musical talent to list on his college applications: guitar teacher to local elementary students. “My favorite part is when I can find a song that they like or that I like, and they play it for the first time,” Stratman said. “It’s a really good feeling to see them excited. I remember that excitement. You finally get it down and it sounds like a song. It’s cool to see that on their faces. I’m reliving my experience of learning the guitar through them,” he added. Stratman taught himself to play guitar after finding one in his grandparents’ closet three years ago. Now he shares his skill each week with four beginning guitarists, meeting them PHS Senior Connor Stratman online or physically distanced in their backyards, even though it’s challenging to teach proper finger positioning or stances from a screen or six feet away. Nonetheless, it’s going well. “I like him a lot,” said one student, 10-year-old Ben McMurtry, who’s learning “Back in Black” by AC/ DC. “I like how he teaches me. It’s fun to play guitar with him.” The lessons come at an important time, when PUSD students are tired of distance learning from home, fourth graders are all playing recorders, and music education is optional for fifth graders. “I hope it’s fun for them to do a little bit something different,” said Stratman, who discovered a love of music when he was about his students’ ages. “I think it’s good to have a little bit of music going on for them in some way.” Kristen Hatcher is a member of the Piedmont Arts Fund, which supports visual and performing arts programs for all PUSD students. articles.text: January 22: $3.2 million was raised by Piedmont Education Fund for Piedmont schools through its annual Giving Campaign. The 17-week fundraiser set a record. January 24: Former Piedmont resident Linda Lei leads all 7th grade students through an intro lesson in Chinese brush paintings. February 6: Piedmont participates in state-wide rally “Fund Public Education Now!”, at the Community Hall. This public gathering of 75 people would be one of the last of the year. February 8: An all-girls Piedmont robotic team “Roses and Rivets” wins the Judges Award at the FIRST Tech Challenge Robotics Tournament in Napa. March 13: Piedmont’s School Board is the first in Alameda County to announce closure of its schools. MARCH 16: All Piedmont schools close due to COVID-19. Alameda County Department of Health initially orders schools closed for two weeks. Middle and High school students are still tasked with some school work via online work on Schedulicity. March 25: Alameda County Office of Education extends the closure of all schools in the county to May 1 to slow the spread of COVID-19. March 25: Supt. Randy Booker states that the California Department of Education will not require schools to comply with the requirement to have a minimum of 180 instructional days during the school year. He confirmes that the school district had made no plans to extend the school year into June to help make up for the lost days of instruction, nor did it have any plans to conduct summer school. Piedmont classes are scheduled to end on Friday, May 29, for summer vacation. March 27: Four Piedmont teens start Feedmont.org, a program to deliver groceries and other essentials to high-risk Piedmonters who want to avoid going into stores. The Feedmont Team is comprised of sophomore Atticus Lim and three seniors, his sisters Natalie and Diana Lim, and Amelia Costello. March 31: California State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond announces schools in California will not reopen before fall 2020. April 20: Class grading for the Spring semester is changed to Pass/No Pass. April 27: Led by incoming Senior Class President Audrey Edel, Piedmont High School students create a Virtual Mentor Program that connects high schoolers and elementary schoolers through crafts, tutoring, and reading. May 12: California State University (CSU), the largest public college system in the country with 23 campuses and 480,000 students, is the first college to announce all classes in fall will be online. May 13: The School Board decides to move forward with demolition of the 10’s building on the high school campus, to be replaced with the new Alan Harvey Theater. May 13: Sue Smegal, a former Piedmont Middle School teacher, School Board member and a longtime volunteer in the schools and community, is presented with the Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award by the School Board. May 14: State School Superintendent Tony Thurmond announces that the decision of when and how to reopen public schools will be left to each school district. May 19: PHS Senior Awards ceremony takes place online. The following seniors won multiple awards: Sophia Zalewski (4): Excellence in Mathematics Plaque, Outstanding Girl Athlete Trophy (Cross Country), Piedmont Certificate in Mandarin, Valedictorian Plaque. Anne Cheng (3): Dean Faberman Plaque (Mock Trial), Spanish for Excellence Trophy and English Trophy. Sophia Butler (2): Outstanding Senior in Drama Director’s Plaque and Susan Kawaichi Plaque Diversity Award. May 21: The University of California suspends the requirement of SAT scores for next year’s applicants, and discontinues the requirement of letter grades for academic classes taken in winter, spring and summer terms of 2020. May 25: The PHS Parents Club hosts a drive-thru for students to pick up their yearbooks and graduation caps and gowns. For many, this was the first in-person school function since March. May 28: Piedmont Middle School has online graduation ceremony through Youtube. No student speeches were given by class Valedictorian Sophia Zalewski or co-Salutatorians Diana Lim and Natalie Lim. June 4: School Reopening Task Force holds its first meeting with nearly 100 participants, including students, parents, classified employees, certificated educators, administrators, and two board members. June 9: The demolition of the administrative and classroom “10s building” begins. In its place will be a new $20 million theater building scheduled for completion Fall of 2021. It takes four Staff photo Piedmont High School’s 3-story classroom building was certified for occupancy by the State on October 16, 2020, two months after its scheduled opening. days to demolish the building. June 24: Governor Newsom announces Assembly Bill 77, which sets requirements for distance learning. Requirements are now in place for attendance, participation and daily teacher interaction with students. A portion of the bill limits distance learning only to certain at-risk students in the fall. “The idea of [full] distance learning is essentially pulled off the table for board consideration,” said Supt. Booker June 26: “Piedmont Partners” starts a petition to reopen schools in the fall. 740 parents, students and community members sign in the first four days. June 30: The School Board votes for a hybrid learning model for the 2020-21 school year during a nearly eight-hour meeting. The board approves in-person classes four or five days per week with face coverings and six foot spacing while breaking classes up into smaller cohorts when possible. July 8: Piedmont High School seniors Audrey Edel, Sadie Tschider, and Anthony Wong start “PiedmontMaskProject,” creating videos and social media posts to spread mask wearing awareness. July 13: The School Board directs the superintendent to start the school year online, citing increases in Bay Area COVID cases. July 17: Governor Newsom forbids public schools from opening if their county is on the COVID “watch-list,” (now equivalent to the purple tier). Alameda County has been on list since July 12. August 7: Five candidates vie for three seats on the School Board. Cory Smegal (incumbent), Hari Titan, Veronica Thigpen, Hilary Cooper, and Jason Kelley file applications to run. August 17: The opening of the STEAM building has been delayed. According to ongoing PUSD announcements, it had been on track to be completed by August 17, August 17: The first day of class begins with online classes, now requiring mandatory attendance and scheduled screen time. A chrome book is given to every student K-12. Parents and students give feedback that online learning has improved from spring. August 26: The school district reaches a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with school employees and (MOU) with teachers solely for Distance Learning. Teachers receive guarantee that in-person learning for TK-5th grade will not start until at least October 1. September 9: After months of deliberation and adapting to state and local policy changes, Piedmont teachers and PUSD strike a tentative agreement on an MOU for in-person learning. Teachers are given the right to dismiss any student not wearing a mask properly; cohort sizes are limited to 15. Exposure to someone with COVID-19 requires a 14-day quarantine and a return to distance learning. An unpaid administrative leave can be requested if a teacher is unable to return to in-person instruction because either they or someone in their household is at increased risk from COVID-19. Risk elements include being over 65 or having a BMI over 30. This agreement goes into effect if schools are allowed to open in the red tier. September 9: The School Board approves development of a Racial Equity policy, which creates an administrative position in the school district, a Director of Equity. A focus is placed on anti-racism policy; curriculum and hiring practices will also change. September 11: The high school student body leaders (ASB) hold a virtual Club Day during lunch. A record-high 39 clubs sign up. September 22: Alameda County moves to red tier. Alameda County schools would have the green light to open after two weeks in red tier, raising hopes that schools in town might finally be able to open. September 23: With a narrow 3-2 vote the School Board agrees to file a waiver with the county to allow TK-5th grade students back in school, regardless of COVID tier. The District will have to show it has testing, safety precautions and a reopening plan. Staying in the red tier looks like a more promising route to schools opening. The waiver program is later canceled by the County. October 6: The School Board approves a new school reopening plan. TK-2 students will return to class on November 3. Grades 3-5 plan to return November 10. October 9: Elementary school families are sent surveys to choose between in-person or distance learning. 75 percent choose in-person. October 12: Bradley Smet from San Luis Obispo is hired as the new high school Athletic Director. October 12: The District posts its reopening plan on the school district website, as part of the requirement to reopen. October 16: STEAM building receives Certificate of Occupancy 2 months after the projected open date. Teachers wait to be allowed in. October 16: Piedmont Makers donate 30 LEGO Mindstorms Robotics sets to Piedmont Middle School to create engineering and programming courses at PMS. The retail value is $18,000. October 23: Just 11 days before the scheduled reopening of schools, Supt. Booker announces a delay from November 3 to December 1 for the return to elementary school campuses due to the district’s inability to create a master school schedule. Teachers opting out of in-person teaching or still unsure leaves the district understaffed. November 3: Cory Smegal, Veronica Thigpen and Hilary Cooper are elected to school board. November 9: Alameda County allows secondary schools to reopen with protocols in place. Supt. Booker announces that the earliest time Piedmont secondary schools could open would be January 4.

articles.text: A parent called me the other day in a panic. “I’m worried that my son is falling behind in school because of Covid,” he said, in obvious distress. “Behind who?” I replied, giving him some time to consider my response. After a moment I added, “Every kid on the planet is in the same boat.” “Oh,” he said, with a little chuckle. “I see what you mean.” While there is nothing funny about the ways Covid is wreaking havoc on education, I believe that we are missing perhaps the only opportunity for optimism during this crisis by focusing on our children’s academic achievement rather than on their spiritual growth, of which there has been plenty in the past several months. Because of Covid, our kids are becoming Spiritual Warriors right before our eyes, and it’s an amazing thing to see. To me, Spiritual Warriors are those who effectively engage their mind, heart, and soul as they navigate the world. It’s a skill set, and Spiritual Warriors toggle among these aspects of themselves and recognize on a deep, perhaps subconscious level, that they must utilize all of these parts of themselves in order to thrive. And make no mistake: Spiritual Warriors are born of adversity, and these days we’ve got plenty of that. To practice the skills of a Spiritual Warrior, we must accept that adversity is inevitable, open our hearts as we journey through it, and allow ourselves to be transformed in the process. Before Covid, many of the students and parents I work with might have defined adversity as struggling to get an A in math, or training hard only to make the JV soccer team. While these are real issues for many kids, facing and overcoming them do not a Spiritual Warrior make. These are mere bumps in the psychological road for the average middle class kid. For the Covid generation, however, the days of these being significant challenges are long gone. For many of my students, Covid is the first situation in their lives where they, and their parents, have absolutely no control. They can’t problem-solve the pandemic way, or spend money (if they have it) to escape it. Covid is a hard stop. And accepting that there are forces greater than us at play is an essential step in our spiritual development. Early in the pandemic, one of my students, Jed, just couldn’t get his mind around the fact that life as he knew it had come to an end. He was angry with his parents for restricting his behavior, and he didn’t want to accept that his actions had consequences beyond his own health and well-being. He accused his parents of treating him unfairly, and they turned to me to see if I could help. “I don’t see what the big deal is,” Jed told me on a Zoom call. “I just want to visit my friends.” “Of course you do,” I replied, “and they want to see you too. But I think you understand why you can’t, right?” It wasn’t that Jed didn’t understand what a pandemic was, or that being out in the world was risky – he did, he’s a smart kid. It was that he didn’t want to feel so helpless, so small, in the face of such a powerful adversary. “How are your friends doing?” I asked, shifting the focus of our conversation a bit. I knew how important Jed’s friends were to him, and how he relied on them. “Well,” he said, “I think they’re having a really rough time.” “I bet they are,” I agreed. “I wonder if you can help?” Jed then talked about one of his friends who he knew was having a particularly hard time. She had a sister with cancer, and the entire family was naturally terrified about her catching the virus. “Maybe I could send her a care package,” Jed suggested after considering how scared and lonely his friend must be. “And make a TikTok video to cheer her up.” Jed did this soon afterwards, and he continues to focus his energy on helping this friend – and others. His parents report he hasn’t gotten angry at them about the pandemic since. For another student, Nadine, Covid hit hard. Being at home, isolated, made her doubt herself, and the self-confidence she had steadily developed throughout adolescence seemed to slip away. She had trouble focusing on her schoolwork, and Zoom was a disaster for her. Having to watch herself on video all day long made her extremely self-conscious. Things came to a head when she had a falling out with a school friend, which left her feeling even lonelier than ever. Nadine felt her school friends didn’t understand her anymore, and so she reached out to an old friend she was connected to on social media. She was heartened to learn that this friend was experiencing the same things she was –isolation and disconnection – and they started communicating every day. Through this friend she has met several others, and now she has a solid group of friends she connects with several times a day. “I never would have found these new friends if it wasn’t for Covid,” Nadine explained to me. “Covid is the worst,” she continued, “but I feel like I’ve finally found my people.” Experiences of surrender carve us, and while we are all being shaped by Covid, for our children, this is a formative experience. Covid will define their generation. Luckily, they are going through this together, even in their isolation from each other, and from what I have witnessed among my own students, I feel confident about the future. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who learn and think differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: Phil Witte is an author and cartoonist. His cartoon “Flip” first appeared in the Piedmont Post in 2008 and now runs in every issue. His cartoons have appeared in dozens of publications in the U.S. and U.K., including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, Reader’s Digest, San Francisco Chronicle, New Statesman, and Private Eye, as well as in books and greeting cards. articles.text: San Francisco Ballet is presenting A Midsummer Night’s Dream from January 21 through February 10. Choreographer George Balanchine’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream is part of San Francisco Ballet’s 2021 digital season and will be performed in Program 1. The ballet, one of the company’s most well-known, is a Shakespearean favorite making its triumphant return to San Francisco after a cut-too-short run in 2020. This 1962 ballet, set to the music of Felix Mendelssohn, was Balanchine’s first original full-length ballet, which quickly was hailed as a masterpiece. Balanchine loved the original play – he could recite large parts of it in Russian – so the ballet sticks close to its inspiration. It tells the story of four lost lovers in the woods, as well as of a royal fairy court made up of Queen Titania, King Oberon, and mischievous Puck. To obtain tickets to this digital event, visit https://www.sfballet. org/tickets/2021-season/.

articles.text: Can a crisis evoke from us a one-shot pinnacle of creativity? In the case of two Austrian villagers some 200 years ago, the answer is an emphatic yes. It was in the small church of Oberndorf, Austria, near Salzburg, readying for the gala Christmas Eve service. The all-important pipe organ broke down, with no chance for repairs being done in time. To compensate for the crisis, the young priest Josef Mohr pulled out his poetic text now known as the sacred lullaby “Silent Night,” calming words for the Christ child in the manger, “Sleep in heavenly peace.” He passed these along to the village school-teacher Franz Gruber, who was suddenly the superfluous church organist. The very same day Gruber (1787-1863) produced the music to fit the voices— equally straight-forward, but uniquely memorable. He scored it for a pair of soloists, chorus and the best substitute instrument available, the guitar. Gruber called his effort “a simple composition.” The parishioners crowded in that night were treated to the 1818 world premiere of a work with singers who had barely had time to rehearse. Later the work was taken up by the Strasser Sisters singing group specializing in Tyrolean music, as well as the Rainers. It became a hit all over the touring itineraries, eventually attributed to the eminent composer Michael Haydn (brother of Franz Josef Haydn). Who, after all, would believe that two village nobodies could create great music? After 15 years it was finally published, and another six years later was already being heard in New York City. For decades uncertainty reigned about the carol’s creators. It took a court-room trial 26 years after the premiere to establish the truth, when Gruber’s son brought in a copy of the original manuscript to prove the true authorship before a governmental investigation committee. Case closed. Any thoughts that Gruber-Mohr could become the Austrian Rodgers and Hammerstein, or Lerner-Loewe, would be sheer fantasy. After 1818 they went their separate ways, given the usual moves and transfers, and never produced other significant works. It was sheer coincidence that the two were together at all; Mohr (1792-1848) had been sent to Oberndorf from his earlier posting because his delicate health could not cope with a harsh climate. Shortly before the Millennium, the sole manuscript regarding the carol’s origins was discovered, written in Mohr’s handwriting, dating back to 1820 or thereabouts. He attested that he had written the texts in 1816, with the music composed by Gruber in 1818. The lesson here is profound and invaluable: The Mozarts and Leonardos of our world could be brilliant every single day. As for the rest of us, however mediocre in the greater scale of things, we could still rise up once in full flower, like a century plant. We could create something uniquely masterful, provided we possess the will, the faith and the motivation. From adversity comes the flowering of inspiration. And a catalytic pairing doesn’t hurt, either. A Piedmont resident, Paul Hertelendy also writes on classical music in the arts journal www.artsSF.com.

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora in San Francisco is presenting a digital exhibition entitled Meet Us Quickly: Painting for Justice from Prison on view until January 31 The Museum of the African Diaspora in San Francisco, a Smithsonian affiliate, is presenting a digital exhibition entitled Meet Us Quickly: Painting for Justice from Prison, which will be on view until January 31. Meet Us Quickly is an exhibition of the work of 12 artists incarcerated at San Quentin State Prison. The twenty-one works in the exhibition include linocut prints, acrylic paintings, ink drawings on paper, and collage and are organized and curated by Prison Renaissance co-founder Rahsaan “New York” Thomas. Eclectic in influence, certain works in this exhibition nod to pointillism and neo-constructivism while others honor the importance of Aaron Douglas and the Harlem Renaissance. These artists maintain significant artistic practices spanning diverse techniques and subjects. The works are presented with accompanying statements written by each artist, allowing these incarcerated men to speak for themselves and share their vision and perspectives in their own words. The exhibition is made possible in part by a grant from The Creative Work Fund, a program of the Walter and Elise Haas Fund that also is supported by The William and Flora Hewlett Foundation. Eighty percent of proceeds from the auction go directly to artists based on the payment method of their choice. To view the artwork, visit https://www. prisonrenaissance.org/art-auction-2020.

articles.text: Led by House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of San Francisco, Congress passed legislation on December 22 providing much-needed shortterm financial relief for nonprofit arts and culture organizations throughout the U.S. It was part of the latest relief bill that both the House and Senate voted to approve The House Small Business Committee and San Francisco Arts Alliance were leading players in incorporating eligibility for arts and culture organizations. The effort was led by Pelosi and House Small Business Committee Chair Nydia Velazquez to include nonprofit arts organizations in the Save our Stages (SOS) bill and the Payroll Protection Program (PPP). Passage was secured with the partnership of Speaker Pelosi, Senate Minority Leader Sen. Charles Schumer of New York, Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, Rep. Velazquez of Brooklyn, and Sen. Marco Rubio of Florida and a broad bi-partisan support that secured the passage of this COVID-19 relief bill. “The arts and culture sector is an essential vehicle for healing and for driving the equitable and sustainable recovery and regeneration of communities across the nation,” said Deborah Cullinan, co-chair of the San Francisco Arts Alliance and CEO of Yerba Buena Center for the Arts. “As we evolve the ways we bring joy, inspiration, and healing into our hard-hit communities, it is only by working hand-in-hand with our elected officials and policymakers on the federal, state, and local level that we will be able to support our nation’s creative workforce in service of the health and wellbeing of our communities.” “As we move into 2021 and the roll-out of the vaccine, it is our fervent hope that arts and culture organizations will be able to reconnect communities through a return to cultural gatherings,” added Matthew Shilvock, General Director of San Francisco Opera and co-chair of the San Francisco Arts Alliance. “This relief bill supports the broad arts and culture sector in a number of important ways, both in sustaining our arts workers and organizations, and in ensuring greater equity of public access to digital artistic offerings through expanded broadband access. We are deeply grateful for this affirmative expression of support for the arts from Congress. It is critical to bringing back the arts and rebuilding our communities.” This relief package incorporates key components of the US Conference of Mayors Resolution sent to Congress in July 2020,. It reinforced federal policy recommendations advanced by more than 60 national arts organizations calling on Congress to ensure the recovery and survival of essential arts and culture organizational partners, including: ● Inclusion of the nonprofits arts and culture industry in specific relief efforts through the Save our Stages (SOS) federal grants for creative and cultural businesses. ● Extending the duration of unemployment insurance for artists, arts professionals, and self-employed workers whose income has been negatively impacted by COVID-19. ● Extending SBA and Paycheck Protection Program assistance for artists and arts professionals and providing additional forgivable SBA loans to nonprofit arts and culture organizations, self-employed workers, sole proprietors, small LLCs. ● Incentivizing increased contributed support for the arts and culture sector by extending through the 2021 tax year the universal charitable deduction for those that do not itemize their tax returns. ● Enabling equitable participation in artistic, educational, and cultural online activity through ensuring the most vulnerable populations have access to free or low-cost high-speed broadband program offerings. Contributing more than $877.8 billion to the nation’s economy in 2017, the arts and culture sector is an economic engine that directly employs more than 5 million workers nationwide. The current losses sustained by the arts and culture sector throughout the nation as a result of the COVID- 19 pandemic have reached a staggering $14.6 billion as of December 12, 2020. Included among the 26 mayors who introduced and co-signed the resolution to Congress in July 2020 were London Breed (San Francisco), Libby Schaaf (Oakland), Jesse Arreguin (Berkeley), and California mayors in Sacramento, Loa Angeles, San Diego, and San Jose.
articles.title: Congress passes relief bill for non-profit arts organizations

Meet Us Quickly is an exhibition of the work of 12 artists incarcerated at San Quentin State Prison. The twenty-one works in the exhibition include linocut prints, acrylic paintings, ink drawings on paper, and collage and are organized and curated by Prison Renaissance co-founder Rahsaan “New York” Thomas. Eclectic in influence, certain works in this exhibition nod to pointillism and neo-constructivism while others honor the importance of Aaron Douglas and the Harlem Renaissance. These artists maintain significant artistic practices spanning diverse techniques and subjects. The works are presented with accompanying statements written by each artist, allowing these incarcerated men to speak for themselves and share their vision and perspectives in their own words. And as noted below, we also see light fixtures themselves during the day. “Less is more” is a famous maxim attributed to the modernist architect Mies van der Rohe in 1947. It basically means that unadorned simplicity (less) results in a better design aesthetic (more). I think this maxim, while certainly not a universal truth, is especially applicable in the field of lighting, where we too often see projects over-illuminated. It seems to be that the best lighting designs go unnoticed – they just seem to naturally fit in place. This is because the focus of good lighting design is on what is being illuminated, not the illumination itself. Lighting is all about contrast, and subtle contrast is easier for the eye to adapt. Although starker contrast is useful for highlighting, in a small residential city like Piedmont, highlighting should be, and for the most part is, limited. Successful lighting designs often use different and multiple types of light sources (fixtures) for different illumination purposes. Using one tall, strong street light for example to also illuminate an entry will be be much less appealing and effective than using two separate fixtures, one to light the street, and another (or more) to light the entry. The issue of appropriate scale and character also enters into lighting design. The incredible lighting on the new east span of the Bay Bridge with its 65’ high poles is of course not appropriate even for a larger city the size of Oakland, and certainly not for a residential scaled city like Piedmont. Also important is the issue of “light trespass” from one type of light to another such as where residential and commercial uses abut. Instead of worrying about things you can’t control, focus on those you can. articles.text: Marella Guigou, well-known for her daily walks at Witter Field in her crimson Stanford sweatshirt, passed away quietly on Thanksgiving morning, November 26, 2020, in Northbrook, Illinois, where she had been living since 2015. She was 89. Born Marella Rimbach on July 15, 1931, she was the daughter of Pearl and Francis Rimbach and grew up on a farm in Sterling, Massachusetts. After graduating from Cushing Academy in Ashburnham, she attended Clark University in Worcester where she earned a Bachelor of Arts degree. After college she worked as a secretary at Harvard University and began teaching elementary school. She moved to San Francisco where she continued teaching, and where she married Charles (Charlie) Hubbard Guigou on October 19, 1963 at St. Mary the Virgin Episcopal Church. They moved to Piedmont in 1965 and raised a family of two daughters. She resumed her teaching career in 1984 after their older daughter attended Stanford, Charlie’s alma mater. For 10 years she was a reading resource teacher at Garfield Elementary School in Oakland. Throughout her adult life “she was absolutely passionate about education,” recalled Stephanie. After she retired from Oakland School District, she remained close to education and close to home, serving as a volunteer at Wildwood Elementary School, and Piedmont’s other two elementary schools. She had a wide circle of friends through her participation with the League of Women Voters, the Daughters of the American Revolution, Republican Women, Piedmont Community Church, and the many parents’ groups affiliated with the schools. She was a rabid Stanford fan, where her husband and elder daughter attended. She was a regular at Jazzercize classes in Piedmont, often completing the exercises in a room of women 20 years her junior. In addition to doing her daily laps walking the oval; track at Witter Field, she walked around the block every morning and brought her neighbors’ newspapers to their doorstep. Always well informed, she made sure the Piedmont Post was delivered on time each Wednesday. “When the phone rang at 6:05 p.m. on a Wednesday, we always knew it was Marella – politely informing us that she hadn’t received the paper,” recalled Post Editor Gray Cathrall. “She wanted to ‘make sure the paper boy was not sick or injured.’ We enjoyed those humorous conversations with her immensely,” he said. One of her favorite outings was having lunch regularly at Fenton’s Creamery. She became very attached to one of the waiters there who made sure she was well cared for. He later told Marella‘s daughter that the conversations with Marella inspired him to apply to and attend UC Berkeley. “He texted me a couple Marella Guigous passed away on November 26. She was 89. years ago to let me know he had graduated from Cal, and credits Marella with changing his life,” said Stephanie. She celebrated her 89th birthday in July at North Shore Place, a memory care home in Northbrook, Illinois. She maintained a happy life there and was adored by the staff. She told each of them every day how much she loved them. Marella is survived by a daughter, Stephanie Joseph and husband Christopher of Empire, Michigan. She was also the proud and playful grandmother of Logan (Catherine), Courtney and Erin Joseph. She is predeceased by her husband Charlie, who died in 2007, and her younger daughter Pamela, who died in 2017. March 20 Piedmont tennis courts, playgrounds, and two of its sports fields – Beach Field and Coaches Field – were closed. Total coronavirus cases in the Bay Area surpass 50, local death toll reaches double digits, and the global death toll surpassed 10,000 The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and the Treasury Department announced that the federal income tax filing due date has been extended from April 15 to July 15. March 26 The City of Piedmont closed another recreation area. On Thursday, March 26, Hampton Park was closed because people are “continuing to gather in violation of both the letter and the spirit of the shelter-in-place orders which have been issued by the county and state” the city wrote in a press release. Between March 20 and March 26 Piedmont police had to disperse groups from fields, parks and tennis courts at least 14 times, despite the closures, according to the police dispatch office. The Alameda County death toll due to COVID-19 reached four. More than half a million cases are reported worldwide. March 30 CDC Director Robert Redfield said that the agency is now reconsidering the data around mask use by the general public. Redfield made these statements in an interview with National Public Radio on Monday, March 30. “I can tell you that the data and this issue of whether it’s going to contribute [to prevention] is being aggressively reviewed as we speak,” Redfield told NPR. Shelter-in-place restrictions in Alameda County, which were to expire on March 30, were extended to May 1. March 31 In a letter to school leaders, California’s State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond wrote: “Due to the current safety concerns and needs for ongoing social distancing, it currently appears that our students will not be able to return to school campuses before the end of the school year.” April 1 The city closed Piedmont Park to prevent the spread of COVID- 19. The City estimated that the closure could last through May 3 during the shelter-in-place mandate from Alameda County. City Administrator Sara Lillevand ultimately made the decision to close all Piedmont parks after lengthy discussions with all of the City’s senior managers. Lillevand cited two main reasons for the closures. She stated that park closures support the letter and spirit of the shelter in place order, which aims to limit opportunities for community transmission and spread of the novel coronavirus. She added that police enforcement of the order is easier with full closures rather than partial closures. Photo by Jonathan Comeaux May 29: A protestor views a blaze on 7th street in downtown Oakland on a violent night of riots. An estimate of over 8,000 protesters were in the city. April 14 Gov. Newsom laid out a sixpoint framework to gradually lift shelter in place restrictions. April 23 It was the deadliest day for coronavirus so far in California. A total of 1,419 Californians have died from the virus and there are 37,339 confirmed cases of COVID. April 28 The U.S. confirmed it has exceeded 1 million confirmed cases of coronavirus, and 57,608 deaths, more than double the number of deaths of Spain. The U.S total is greater than the total of the next six highest reporting countries in the world. Spain reported 232,128 cases, Italy reported 201,505, France reported 166,036, the United Kingdom reported 162,350 cases, Germany has 159,239, and Turkey has reported 114,653 cases. China, the origin of the virus, reported 83,938 confirmed cases. May 11 Piedmont’s city staff hosted a virtual town hall meeting to answer residents’ questions on mandated lockdowns and restrictions. The Fourth of July parade committee decided to cancel this year’s parade, citing coronavirus concerns, and the inability to gather in large numbers. It was the first time the parade had been canceled and was the first cancellation of a major city event. May 13 Mayor Bob McBain offered an upbeat message to the community: “As we enter the ninth week of this shared experience, it’s important to reflect on these recent times. I was confident that our community would respond strongly and support steps taken to slow the spread of the virus. We are a conscientious and respectful community that understands the issues. Nonetheless, I was still amazed at the overwhelmingly considerate and respectful response of Piedmont residents.” May 19 The Piedmont Recreation Department announced that all originally planned summer camps and classes had been cancelled. The recommendation from the Alameda County Public Health Department for summer camps is to keep “stable groups” together for four weeks, and not have groups of students mix with each other. May 25 A black man in Minnesota, George Floyd, 46, is killed Monday, May 25 at the hands of a white police officer, Derek Chauvin. Floyd was detained, cuffed and brought to the ground after trying to pay with a counterfeit bill at a store. Video captured by pedestrians showed the white officer kneeling on Floyd’s neck for nearly 9 minutes, despite Floyd’s pleas that he couldn’t breathe. The officers involved ultimately were charged with murder, and the event sparked a national maelstrom. The California Department of Public Health announces that places of worship and in-store retail shopping may reopen statewide, subject to some limitations. Places of worship can hold religious services and funerals that limit attendance to 25 percent of a building’s capacity, subject to a maximum of 100 people. The vast majority of public gatherings is still prohibited under the state’s stay-at-home order. Events designed for political expression, such as protests, are allowed for up to 100 people. May 31 Residents of Piedmont organize a peaceful protest throughout the city and into Oakland. Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers marched alongside protestors. “The organizers let [the Police Department] know that they expected a relatively small crowd, and that they would be in the area of Oakland Avenue and Highland Avenue,” Bowers explained. The May 31 event grew much larger than that, as protesters engaged in a march throughout Piedmont. Bowers said that the march was not anticipated, but that the primary focus for his officers was an emphasis on keeping protestors safe and facilitating traffic control. The City of Piedmont imposed a nightly curfew for the week, See Year in Review on page 29 Photo by Rob Yelland May 31: A protestor takes a knee during a march and peaceful protest that began in Piedmont and spilling over into neighboring Oakland.

articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council unanimously approved a first reading of an ordinance which will require the electronic filing of campaign disclosure forms and statements of economic interests. California Governor Gavin Newsom signed a law in September of this year, which goes into effect on January 1, 2021, requiring all campaign filings to be posted on a City’s website within 72 hours of receipt. At the present time, filings are accepted on paper in Piedmont. The law allows local government agencies to require an elected and appointed official, candidate, or committee to file campaign statements, reports, and other documents online or electronically with a local filing officer. City Clerk John Tulloch explained that the proposal seeks to increase election transparency and save staff time. The city selected NetFile software to be the best solution for online filings in the future. The NetFile system is created specifically for cities responsible for administering campaign finance filings and Statements of Economic Interest and allows for electronic and paperless filing of campaign statements. The first reading was unanimously approved. The ordinance will be posted at City Hall after its second reading by the city council for at least 30 days and will become effective 30 days after the second reading.

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council unanimously approved a pilot program to install ‘speed cushions’ on Scenic Avenue and Greenbank Avenue at its December 21 meeting. The section of Scenic Avenue, from Blair Avenue to Alta Avenue, is a narrow street with no sidewalk and limited parking on both sides of the street. “It’s a very confusing and conflict-ridden street with respect to pedestrian safety, being that there are no sidewalks and visibility is compromised,” said recently retired Public Works Director Chester Nakahara. City staff was contacted by residents of Scenic Avenue in 2017 to address traffic concerns related to speed and pedestrian safety. One of their stated goals was to reduce the speed limit on the street from 15 miles per hour to 10 miles per hour. Due to the pandemic and city staff’s bandwidth, further meetings were delayed until October 20, when a virtual meeting was hosted by the city for all residents of the Scenic Avenue neighborhood. Three residents of this group joined in with Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Nakahara, City Engineer John Wanger, and traffic engineer Aaron Elias of Kittelson & Associates. They concluded that lowering the speed limit was not needed. Other options were explored and considered. In a discussion with Bowers and former Fire Chief Bret Black, speed cushions were determined to be the most viable solution. Speed cushions are vertical speed control elements placed in the roadway that are designed to manage traffic speeds. They are generally used on residential or slow-speed streets, where larger freight traffic is discouraged. They are different from speed humps, in that they include wheel cutouts that allow larger vehicles with wider tire spacing to pass through them at regular speeds while forcing passenger cars with narrower wheel spacing to reduce their speeds. A second location, the 200 block of Greenbank Avenue (between Oakland and Grand Avenues), was included in the plan to use speed cushions. The proposed placement of five speed cushions on Scenic are at 150, 210, 237, 266, and 288 Scenic Avenue. The proposed locations for two speed cushions on Greenbank are at roughly 211 and 231 Greenbank Avenue. “The pilot program is really an attempt to collect real-time data and feedback from residents, pedestrians, bicyclists, and allow our public safety vehicles to test the impact on their response time,” Nakahara explained. The cost of seven speed cushions is approximately $15,000, plus installation and required signage at $10,000, bringing the total to approximately $25,000, according to staff reports.

articles.text: Leaves legacy of community events, improved relations with public After seven and a half years with the Piedmont Police Department, and a 22-year career in law enforcement, Sergeant Nicole Bolden has officially retired. Former Piedmont Police Chief Ricki Goede hired Bolden in 2013 and Bolden was promoted to the rank of Sergeant in January 2019. Bolden is not one to sit back and enjoy the ride. She pioneered the department’s community outreach program within Piedmont and in neighboring cities. The programs have gotten Piedmont officers involved with community members. “I have been most committed to community awareness, justice and giving people a forum or voice to speak,’ she said. “Nothing is ever black or white; we have to work together to make sure that everyone gets the justice that they deserve.” Bolden was born and raised in Richmond. Whenever law enforcement showed up, it was related to something negative, she recalls. In her time in Piedmont, Bolden worked for law enforcement to be a positive change in the community. “Sergeant Bolden brought her professional experience along with her personal experiences and passion to increase our Department’s connection with the public. I wish her all the best in the next chapter of her life and thoroughly enjoyed working with her,” said Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. Bolden was instrumental in bringing National Night Out to Piedmont. The nationwide event provides a chance for a casual and friendly mixing of residents with members of the police and fire departments. Residents are encouraged to organize block At her pinning ceremony in January 2019, Piedmont Police Officer Nicole received her Sergeant pin from her future husband, Jeffrey Jennings. parties and barbecues, and officers come to visit as many parties as possible. Bolden was also instrumental in starting Trunk or Treat, an event for Piedmont kids to decorate a patrol vehicle with Halloween decorations, pick up candy and take photos. Bolden expanded the Piedmont Police Department’s involvement to outside of the Piedmont community with “Shop with a Cop” in San Leandro. In this outreach program, Piedmont officers meet up with kids to help them shop at Walmart with donated gift cards. “Sgt. Bolden’s dedication and leadership have had a very positive effect on our community policing efforts. Our police-community relationships have improved based on her efforts,” said her immediate boss, Captain Chris Monahan. Bolden also initiated a partnership with Wednesday Walkers, a group of primarily seniors taking scheduled two-hour walks in town once a week. She saw it as an opportunity to promote public safety and awareness in the community, and led to the campaign. Bolden is also responsible for PPD’s involvement with Adopt a Family and for the partnership with Piedmont Fire Department in a gift-giving campaign called Three Wise Men. “With COVID there are a lot of limitations on any other opportunities. I thought that maybe I would be pursuing a second retirement in investigations, but I’m just going to take it for what it is, and enjoy the time I do have off,” Bolden said. Bolden lives in Sacramento, and recently was married to Jeffrey Jennings, the new Police Chief of the City of Emeryville. “I now have the time to enjoy my family members, who have been a great support and a driving point in my career. My son is in the Navy and my daughter works in the tech field for a San Francisco company,” she explained. “It’s great to leave this department on a high note and as a positive representative of the profession that I chose.” Bolden stated.
articles.title: Sgt. Nicole Bolden retires from police department
